vol2:fig-comm-compute-overlap.purpose: When is a gradient ready for communication and for the optimizer?
storyboard: The GPU is computing L4 gradients. No gradient can be communicated before its backward work completes.
Local g4 is complete. The GPU must pay nonoverlappable overhead o4 before its AllReduce launches.
After o4, g4 is in flight on the network while the GPU computes L3. g4 is not yet safe for the optimizer.
AllReduce L4 has completed within the later backward window. The GPU now holds reduced Σg4 and local g3; o3 precedes its launch.
g3 communicates while the GPU computes L2. The earlier reduced gradient remains live for the later optimizer step.
Σg3 joins Σg4. Local g2 is ready, and o2 still occupies the GPU before the next transfer.
g2 communicates while the GPU computes L1. The same layer cannot hide its own gradient transfer because that gradient was unavailable before backward finished.
All backward work is complete. Local g1 is ready, but o1 and its AllReduce have no remaining backward computation to hide behind.
After o1, g1 communicates while the GPU waits. The optimizer cannot consume local g1 as though it were globally reduced.
Σg1 has arrived. All four required reduced gradients are now available, so the optimizer dependency is satisfied.

The optimizer consumes the completed reduced gradients and updates the parameters. Earlier overlap hid communication only within the illustrated later-compute windows; the final tail remained exposed.
vol2:fig-comm-compute-overlap.guard: AllReduce launches only after gradient readiness and GPU overhead, in fixed L4-to-L1 order. Optimizer waits for all reductions. Hiding a transfer depends on later compute and completion timing; no claim that every real workload hides all but the last bucket.

vol2:fig-federated-averaging-cycle.guard: Only clients 1–4 are timely and accepted. Normalize by their sample counts only. No assertion that all invited clients contribute or that model averaging is an unweighted mean.

vol2:fig-gpudirect-data-path.purpose: Which copies disappear with GPUDirect RDMA?
storyboard: The GPU owns payload G. The registered host buffer is empty; nothing has crossed the network.
G is copied through the PCIe switch and CPU root complex into host memory. The original GPU payload remains.
The NIC reads the host copy through the root complex and PCIe switch. The host buffer has incurred one n-byte write and one n-byte read.
The NIC sends G to the fabric. This path used host staging; transmission still consumes the network.
Reset the comparison to a new independent send. G remains in GPU memory, and the host buffer stays empty.
The NIC reads G directly from GPU memory over the PCIe peer path. Payload bytes still cross this link; only the host bounce is removed.
The NIC sends the same G to the fabric. Host payload traffic is absent, but PCIe and network transfer remain.
vol2:fig-gpudirect-data-path.guard: Host payload traffic disappears only in the direct case. NIC access is still a transfer over PCIe, followed by network transmission; no claim of zero transfer, one DMA transaction, or measured speedup.

vol2:fig-moe-all-to-all-routing.purpose: How does each expert result find its original token?
storyboard: Each rank owns four tokens and records their original positions. The gate assigns one expert to each token.
All sixteen tokens follow the original top-1 assignment. Expert 2 receives a from rank 0; each expert receives one token from every rank.
Each expert transforms its assigned tokens. a becomes a′ at Expert 2. The origin rank and token position stay attached to the result.
The second exchange returns each expert output to its original rank and slot. a′ returns to rank 0, slot a; dispatch destinations are not the output owners.
Each original rank applies its gate weight to its returned outputs. Top-1 has one expert result per token; no second expert contribution is invented.
vol2:fig-moe-all-to-all-routing.guard: Exact original token-to-expert assignment and inverse permutation. Prime denotes expert transformation; output returns to token owner. Top-1 only; no fabricated numeric activation, bandwidth, or load claim.

vol2:fig-pfc-credit-deadlock.purpose: What must change before a deadlocked queue can forward?
storyboard: Each queue holds four packets. Its head packet needs a slot in the next queue clockwise, but no next queue has space.
Each full queue sends PAUSE counterclockwise to its predecessor. Packet forwarding dependencies still point clockwise.
No packet can advance: every head waits for a full downstream queue, and every sender is paused. Waiting alone cannot make space.
An external watchdog drops A0 from queue 1. This is packet loss, not successful delivery. The new free slot allows queue 4 to resume in this declared toy.
D0 advances clockwise from queue 4 into the free slot in queue 1. Queue 4 now has the free slot.
C0 advances clockwise into queue 4. The free slot moves upstream to queue 3.
B0 advances clockwise into queue 3. Queue 2 can now accept a packet.
A1 advances clockwise into queue 2. The cycle has made progress because recovery created space; the discarded A0 still requires transport recovery.
vol2:fig-pfc-credit-deadlock.guard: PAUSE direction is opposite to the packet dependency. No queue drains while all are full. Watchdog drop is recorded as loss; resumption is conditional on the explicitly simplified threshold rule.

vol2:fig-pipeline-parallelism.guard: Canonical F time=s+m; B time=13-s-m. Each stage eight busy/six idle slots. No early backward, byte estimate, or performance extrapolation.

storyboard: The proxy receives R0–R19. Production remains the only authority for user responses.
The proxy sends each input to production and a copy to the isolated candidate. The same request identities appear in both execution paths.
Production outputs return to users. Candidate outputs are logged for comparison and cannot enter the response path.
Both outputs can be compared offline. The candidate has executed the same batch in addition to production, but no user has seen its answers.

Requests R0–R18 go to production; R19 goes to the candidate. This is the declared one-of-twenty illustration of the original 5 percent stage.
Production answers its nineteen requests and the candidate answers R19. Candidate behavior is now exposed to one live user in this toy batch.
The illustrated stage stays at 5 percent until measured evidence supports a change. SLO or error drift requires rollback; shadow comparison alone cannot reveal user reactions to unseen outputs.

vol2:fig-tinytl-architecture.purpose: Why does a frozen backbone still need a backward pass?
storyboard: Both models hold persistent weights. Full fine-tuning marks backbone weights trainable; TinyTL keeps them frozen. No saved input tile is live yet.
Full fine-tuning retains the shown full input for block 1. TinyTL retains the smaller lite-residual input shown for that block; its frozen backbone weights remain available.
Both models advance through block 2 and retain the state needed by its later backward consumers. Earlier saved inputs remain live.
The third block executes. Three block-input records are now live in each schematic, with different state requirements.
The classifier receives its input. Its saved input joins the block records; none can be released before its last backward consumer.
The classifier computes its gradients and passes an activation gradient to block 3. The shown classifier input can now be released.

The activation gradient traverses block 3 in both models. Full fine-tuning forms its weight gradients; TinyTL forms bias and lite-residual gradients without changing the frozen backbone weight. The consumed saved input is released.
Backward traverses the second frozen TinyTL block as well. Only after its consumers finish is its shown saved input released.
Backward reaches the first block in both models. Its saved input is consumed and released. Frozen weights did not truncate gradient propagation.

Full fine-tuning updates all trainable weights. TinyTL updates biases, lite residuals, and the classifier; the backbone weights keep their original values. These tiles are saved inputs, not total training memory.
vol2:fig-tinytl-architecture.guard: Frozen backbone weights never change, but backward traverses all three blocks. Only saved-input state is illustrated; masks, normalization, gradient storage, and total training memory are not quantified. Parameter updates occur only at optimizer step.
